messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Aroha's Reckoning

Aroha was twenty-two when his older brother Matiu died. The funeral was held on a grey Auckland afternoon, and Aroha stood in the chapel wearing his only dark suit, watching his mother's shoulders collapse as the casket was lowered into the ground. Matiu had been drinking that night—had been drinking for months, really, ever since his girlfriend left him—and he'd driven his car into a concrete barrier on the motorway. The police said he was going over a hundred kilometers an hour. Aroha had not been there. He had been home, asleep, and he had woken to his father's voice, tight and fractured, telling him to get to the hospital. But he had been there in other ways: he had known Matiu was in trouble and had said nothing; he had been irritated when Matiu called him at work the week before, had cut the conversation short because he was busy counting pills at the pharmacy. These facts had calcified into certainty over the months that followed.

Two years later, Aroha was still a pharmacist at the Countdown in Ponsonby, still filling prescriptions with mechanical precision, but the world had become a place of hidden threats. His body had learned to respond before his mind could catch up. Last week, a customer had come to the counter reeking of alcohol—not drunk, just someone who'd had a beer with lunch—and Aroha's chest had tightened, his hands had begun to shake, and he'd found himself gripping the edge of the counter. His manager had asked if he was all right. He wasn't. The smell had transported him nowhere and everywhere at once: to the image of Matiu's car twisted around that barrier, to his own failure to answer the phone, to the knowledge that he was alive and his brother was not. The physical reaction had come first—the racing heart, the sense of imminent catastrophe—and only afterward had Aroha's mind caught up with what had triggered it.

These reactions happened constantly now. His body remained in a state of perpetual readiness, as though danger was always seconds away from materializing. He would be restocking shelves and suddenly feel certain that something terrible was about to happen, even as the fluorescent lights hummed overhead and customers browsed the aisles in perfect safety. His nervous system no longer trusted the world to be what it appeared to be. And this constant vigilance fed a darker conviction: that his life had been irreversibly destroyed by what had happened to Matiu. The happiness he'd once felt—the lightness he remembered from his early twenties, before the phone call—seemed to belong to a different person entirely. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. His job was just a job. His flat was just a place to sleep. The future stretched ahead as a grey, empty thing.

When Aroha tried to recall the events surrounding Matiu's death, the narrative fractured. He could remember isolated images—his father's face in the hospital corridor, the priest's voice during the service—but they didn't connect into a coherent story. Sometimes he could access these fragments without feeling anything at all, as though they had happened to someone else and he was simply observing from a great distance. Other times, when he allowed himself to remember, guilt consumed him so entirely that he had to stop and sit down. The memory itself had become a trigger: thinking about what he should have done differently, about the phone call he'd cut short, would send him spiraling into that same bodily panic. And the triggers kept multiplying. Funerals announced in the news made him nauseous. The cemetery near his flat, which he'd always cut through as a shortcut, had become impossible to pass. Worst of all were the moments when he witnessed someone behaving badly—someone being cruel or selfish or reckless—and his mind would flash to Matiu's choices, to the moral weight of his own inaction, and his body would respond as though he himself were in mortal danger.

He had begun to avoid more and more. He'd stopped going out on weekends. He'd asked his manager if he could work the early shifts, when the pharmacy was quieter and he was less likely to encounter unexpected triggers. His mother had stopped calling as often because he never answered. The avoidance had become its own kind of trap, narrowing his world further with each passing week, and he could feel something breaking inside him—not suddenly, but the way a dam breaks, one small fracture spreading into larger ones. It was this sense of his own unraveling that finally brought him to the clinic, though he could barely articulate what he wanted help with. He only knew that the person he had been was gone, and the person he had become was someone he no longer recognized.
